A *flow log record* represents a network flow in your VPC. By default, each record captures a network IP traffic flow that occurs within an aggregation interval. Each record is a string with fields separated by spaces. A record includes values for the different components of the IP flow, for example, the source, destination, and protocol. When you create a flow log, you can use the default format for the flow log record, or you can specify a custom format. For more information, see Flow log record examples (Amazon VPC documentation).\\\\n\\\\nFlow logs don\\'t capture the following information:\\\\n\\\\n* Traffic generated by instances when they contact the Amazon Domain Name System (DNS) server. After you create a flow log, you can retrieve and view the flow log records in CloudWatch Logs in the log group that you configure. For example, you can\\'t associate a different IAM role\\\\n with the flow log, or add or remove fields in the flow log record. Instead, you\\\\n can delete the flow log and create a new one with the required configuration.\\\\n* If your network interface has multiple IPv4 addresses and traffic is sent to a\\\\n secondary private IPv4 address, the flow log displays the primary private IPv4\\\\n address in the `dstaddr` field. To capture the original destination\\\\n IP address, create a flow log with the `pkt-dstaddr` field.\\\\n* If traffic is sent to a network interface and the destination is not any of\\\\n the network interface\\'s IP addresses, the flow log displays the primary private\\\\n IPv4 address in the `dstaddr` field. To capture the original\\\\n destination IP address, create a flow log with the `pkt-dstaddr`\\\\n field.\\\\n* If traffic is sent from a network interface and the source is not any of the\\\\n network interface\\'s IP addresses, the behavior depends on the flow direction.\\\\n For an egress flow, the flow log displays the primary private IPv4 address in\\\\n the `srcaddr` field. Amazon VPC captures Traffic Mirroring data in the [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs.html) on the destination network interface or Network Load Balancer.\\\\n\\\\nFlow logs have the following [limitations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs-limitations.html):\\\\n\\\\n* Flow logs sample data but don\\'t perform a full packet capture.\\\\n* Flow logs don\\'t capture the packet contents, only metadata.\\\\n* Amazon VPC sends flow logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), where the logs require additional processing.\\\\n\\\\nTo get information about your Traffic Mirroring data from VPC Flow Logs, complete the following steps:\\\\n\\\\n1. {"id": "8a0d78de-c11b-4971-ad21-183bca735f99", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Good news — this confirms what I suspected: finding nothing doesn't mean the DNS queries are failing. It's actually expected behavior.

**VPC Flow Logs explicitly exclude DNS traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS resolver.** Per AWS documentation, flow logs don't capture:
- Traffic generated by instances contacting the Amazon DNS server (the VPC resolver)
- Instance metadata traffic, DHCP, Windows activation, and a few other categories

So an empty result for `i-0abc123def456789` querying the VPC resolver is exactly what you'd expect to see whether the queries are succeeding or failing — flow logs simply aren't the right tool to observe that traffic.

**Caveat:** this only applies to the *Amazon-provided* resolver (the `.2` address). If the instance is using a custom/self-managed DNS server instead, that traffic **is** captured in flow logs normally.

**To actually check whether DNS queries from this instance are succeeding or failing**, you'd want:
- **Route 53 Resolver Query Logging** — logs the actual DNS queries and responses per instance/source IP, which is the purpose-built tool for this
- Or check resolution directly from the instance (e.g., `dig`/`nslookup` against the resolver) if you have access

Want me to check whether Route 53 Resolver query logging is already enabled for this VPC, or look into the instance another way?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
